scope: Ordinary social scenes, institutional standing interfaces and rival/faction turn procedures. Not full setting, historical eras or cosmology review. No new mechanic or current source change.

questions.title: Declare the scene before rolling
questions.question: Keep the Director Want/Leverage/Limit/Clock/Witness frame. Specify the actual requested outcome, who can decide it, available offer/threat, genuine opportunity and disclosed consequence. Define when no check is needed or no current approach can obtain the requested concession; a high roll does not create authority, knowledge or a missing prerequisite.

questions.title: Three narrative results and four native task degrees
questions.question: The manual asks for full success, costly success and refusal/reversal. Reviewed Core uses four fixed-DC task degrees with natural shifts and separate opposed-total ties. Decide exactly which roll procedure applies and how each actual result selects a predeclared narrative outcome. Do not import automatic natural20 obedience, extra degree benefits, hidden tie modifiers or binary-save critical rules.

questions.title: Skills and actual information
questions.question: Preserve Persuasion/willingness, Deception/believed information, Intimidation/perceived risk and Insight/understanding, while accounting for actual Performance and Reputation skills in the Player source and20-skill foundation. Define fixed DC versus opposed checks and limits of truthful information, misunderstanding, credible threats and investigation. Insight is not a generic lie detector; identify any proposed completion as NEW.

questions.title: Third reputation table and automatic modifier routing
questions.question: Extend existing FL-23 with the actual Player Revered+5/Respected+3/Friendly+1/Neutral0/Suspicious-1/Hostile-3/Hated-5 modifier table, whose labels differ from the Loop standing/access table and runtime bands. Settle standing-based access versus an added check modifier, and whether Reputation skill proficiency is a distinct source so standing is not accidentally counted twice. Preserve original scores and labels.

questions.title: Alignment paragraph receipt and pre-push boundary
questions.question: The adjacent original Player paragraph gives identical/compatible/opposing alignment advantage rules and incompatible terminology. Preserve the entire paragraph as evidence without interpreting cosmic alignment or inventing a compatibility chart. Identify any already reviewed controlling decision; otherwise explicitly route unresolved meanings to the post-push review and give the ordinary social procedure an honest dependency boundary. Do not infer a new universal social bonus from alignment lore.

questions.title: Communication, participation and elapsed time
questions.question: Apply fulfilled LAX hearing/speech/signed/textual/interpretation and six-second in-encounter limits. Define one scene clock across speakers, interpreters and physically separate participants; roleplay length is not automatic fictional elapsed time. Actual language, sensory and source-specific comprehension prerequisites still apply. Silence, incapacity or a blocked channel cannot be erased by a social skill roll.

questions.title: Assistance, repetition and changed leverage
questions.question: Define eligible assistance and group participation under the current Help/action rules, and whether a second attempt with unchanged facts is available. One scene should not become unlimited independent retries by rotating speakers. State what genuinely changed evidence, cost, deadline or approach makes another attempt meaningful; preserve paid resources and prior consequences.

questions.title: Social magic and source-specific agency
questions.question: Carry actual Charmed/Frightened limits, fulfilled spell procedures and each acquired class feature in full. Charmed alone is not obedience or consent; intimidation is not automatically Frightened. Source-specific magical control retains its own eligibility, cost, save, ending, awareness and immunity rules. Keep remaining pending spells unavailable and avoid promoting class/card comparison records. Identify exact named hook conflicts for a separate disposition.

questions.title: NPC agreement and player table boundaries
questions.question: Preserve actual authority, non-negotiable limits and the reviewed Session Zero agreement when characters bargain, threaten or disagree. Separate fictional pressure from a player table agreement and from explicit willing-recipient requirements on effects. A social result must not manufacture a resource, bind an absent owner or override the actual consent prerequisite of another procedure.

questions.title: Witnesses, attributed events and standing changes
questions.question: The Director changes standing after public, significant, attributable actions and distinguishes one NPC relationship from a faction. The Loop also gives scene-based numeric caps. Route numeric resolution to FL-23 and its preservation addendum; complete actual witness/evidence/event recording, timing and independent faction responses without assuming every rumor is true or globally known.

questions.title: Faction-turn cadence and paid world actions
questions.question: The manual gives up to three watched factions one action after each return to Haven/surface. Define the genuine event, fictional interval, eligibility, repeat-return guard and what actual resources/access an action requires. Rival actions must use actual routes/information/time. Prevent repeated boundary crossings or one actor on two fronts from generating free faction actions; distinguish a Director abstraction from simulated runtime.

questions.title: Rival clocks and usable faction records
questions.question: Retain the full rival sheet and Depth4–8/Claim4/Grudge4/Collapse4–6 source clocks. Supply finite trigger, tick amount, duplicates, completion and visible-consequence rules; a tick cannot authenticate secret information or erase a real journey. Distinguish44 generic runtime standing IDs from actual named institutions/Expeditions with goals, resources and relations. Produce a source-linked scene/faction record and full ordinary worked sequence. No new world faction history or cosmological truth follows from these fields.

blocks.text: Chapter 36 — Rival Expeditions and Faction Turns

Rivals make the Opening move when the player characters are not looking. They are most effective when they are competent, understandable, and capable of cooperation as well as betrayal. A rival that exists only to steal kills or mock the party will become tedious. A rival with overlapping goals creates decisions.
The Rival Expedition Sheet

rows: Line they claim they will not cross
What they need from the party
What they fear the party will learn

blocks.text: Rival Competence

Give a rival one thing it does better than the player Expedition and one thing it does worse. The Gilded Wake may have superior funding and weak field discipline. The Ashen Lanterns may map brilliantly but lack healing. This creates credible exchanges and prevents rivals from feeling like omnipotent Director avatars.
The Faction Turn

After each return to a haven or the surface, choose up to three watched factions. Each takes one action: recruit, denounce, buy, raid, research, fortify, bargain, conceal, or wait. Resolve the action at the level players can perceive. A faction may advance a private project, but the next session should contain a rumor, price shift, messenger, missing person, new guard presence, or other visible sign.
Rival Clocks

rows: Time passes, the party shares maps, or the rival gains support
Rival reaches a contested node or Gate
Rival gathers proof, witnesses, or legal support
Rival controls salvage, route, or public credit
Humiliation, loss, betrayal, or public accusation
Rival acts directly against the party
Casualties, debt, internal conflict, or exposure
Rival fractures, bargains desperately, or becomes dangerous

blocks.text: When Rivals Win

Let rivals achieve objectives. Their victories prove the world is moving and create new situations: the route is open but taxed, the relic is already sold, a Gate has been disturbed, or a rival survivor needs rescue. Do not erase the player campaign. A rival victory changes the objective rather than making play irrelevant.

rows: Rivals Know Only What They Could Learn

Do not use rival Expeditions to deliver Director knowledge, perfectly counter player plans, or appear wherever the story needs friction. Track their routes, information sources, and time. Fair rivals are more threatening because players can understand how they succeeded.

blocks.text: Chapter 44 — Social Conflict and Reputation Scenes

A social scene becomes a conflict when someone wants an outcome the other side has reason to resist. Roleplay determines approach and information; checks resolve uncertainty. Reputation determines the starting field and what outcomes are plausible. A Honored Expedition may be heard without an appointment. A Hated one may need leverage merely to enter the room.
The Social Scene Frame

rows: What does each side want before the scene ends?
What can each side offer, reveal, threaten, or withhold?
What will each side not agree to under current conditions?
What changes if the conversation takes too long?
Who will hear about the outcome?

blocks.text: Three Results, Not Two

Prepare a full success, costly success, and refusal or reversal. Costly success is not a disguised failure; the party gets the requested access or agreement but owes a favor, accepts oversight, loses secrecy, pays more, or grants credit. Refusal should open another path: new leverage, a different faction, illegal entry, or delayed opportunity.
Using Skills

Persuasion changes willingness, Deception changes believed information, Intimidation changes perceived risk, and Insight changes what the character understands. No single skill controls another person’s mind. A perfect argument cannot make an NPC betray the one value the scene established as non-negotiable, though it may reveal what would change that limit.
Reputation Movement

Move reputation after actions that are public, significant, and attributable. Private kindness may change one NPC without changing a faction. A witnessed Gate victory, broken treaty, rescue, theft, or public accusation can shift a tier. Record why the movement occurred; later NPCs should react to the story, not the number alone.
Reputation in Aethel

Your Reputation reflects how you are perceived by the various factions, settlements, and influential figures across Aethel. It is a dynamic score, influenced by your background, actions, alignment, and affiliations. High reputation with a group can unlock quests, provide discounts, grant access to restricted areas, or earn you valuable allies. Conversely, low reputation can lead to hostility, suspicion, increased prices, or outright refusal of service.
Starting Reputation: Your chosen Background often provides a starting positive or negative reputation with specific groups relevant to your past.

Gaining/Losing Reputation: Completing quests, making significant choices, demonstrating your alignment through actions (helping the needy vs. exploiting the weak), associating with certain NPCs, and even succeeding or failing certain social skill checks can all modify your reputation scores with various factions.
Reputation Tiers: Reputation often functions in tiers (e.g., Hated, Disliked, Neutral, Liked, Honored), with each tier unlocking different interactions and consequences.

Alignment Influence: Actions consistent with your alignment tend to improve reputation with like-minded factions and decrease it with opposing ones. A Good character consistently acting selflessly will gain reputation with temples and righteous orders but lose it with thieves' guilds or dark cults.
Managing your reputation is crucial for navigating the complex social and political landscape of Aethel.
Charisma Checks

A Charisma check might arise when you try to influence or entertain others, when you try to make an impression or tell a convincing lie, or when you are navigating a tricky social situation. The Deception, Intimidation, Performance, Persuasion, and Reputation skills reflect aptitude in certain kinds of Charisma checks.

Deception. Your Charisma (Deception) check determines whether you can convincingly hide the truth, either verbally or through your actions. This deception can encompass everything from misleading others through ambiguity to telling outright lies. Typical situations include trying to fast-talk a guard, con a merchant, earn money through gambling, pass yourself off in a disguise, dull someone's suspicions with false assurances, or maintain a straight face while telling a blatant lie.

Intimidation. When you attempt to influence someone through overt threats, hostile actions, and physical violence, the Director might ask you to make a Charisma (Intimidation) check. Examples include trying to pry information out of a prisoner, convincing street thugs to back down from a confrontation, or using the edge of a broken bottle to convince a sneering noble to reconsider a decision.
Performance. Your Charisma (Performance) check determines how well you can delight an audience with music, dance, acting, storytelling, or some other form of entertainment.

Persuasion. When you attempt to influence someone or a group of people with tact, social graces, or good nature, the Director might ask you to make a Charisma (Persuasion) check. Typically, you use persuasion when acting in good faith, to foster friendships, make cordial requests, or exhibit proper etiquette. Examples of persuading others include convincing a chamberlain to let your party see the king, negotiating peace between warring tribes, or inspiring a crowd of townsfolk.

Reputation. Your Charisma (Reputation) check reflects how well you can leverage your standing with various factions and communities throughout Aethel. This might involve calling in favors, being recognized for past deeds, or using your influence to open doors that would otherwise remain closed.
Other Charisma Checks. The Director might call for a Charisma check when you try to accomplish tasks like the following:
* Find the best person to talk to for news, rumors, and gossip
* Blend into a crowd to get the sense of key topics of conversation
Reputation and Alignment Interactions
In Decennium Descent, your character's reputation with various factions and their alignment can significantly impact ability checks in social situations.
Reputation Modifiers
When interacting with NPCs affiliated with specific factions, your reputation level with that faction can provide bonuses or penalties to Charisma-based ability checks:
* Revered (+5): You're a legendary figure to this faction
* Respected (+3): You're well-known and trusted
* Friendly (+1): You're viewed positively
* Neutral (0): No modifier
* Suspicious (-1): You're viewed with caution
* Hostile (-3): You're actively distrusted
* Hated (-5): You're considered an enemy
Alignment Compatibility
Your alignment relative to an NPC's alignment can also affect social interactions:
* Identical Alignment (advantage on Charisma checks)
* Compatible Alignment (no modifier)
* Opposing Alignment (disadvantage on Charisma checks)

Remember that Good and Evil alignments are fundamentally incompatible in Aethel, while Harmony and Discord can work together despite tension. Neutral characters can bridge these divides, serving as mediators between opposing forces.
These reputation and alignment systems add depth to social encounters in Aethel, making your character's standing in the world and moral choices mechanically significant beyond combat situations.
